section.title: The Fountain of Cleansing and the Struck Shepherd
section.sectionRationale: The mourning of chapter 12 flows straight into cleansing. On that day a fountain is opened for sin and impurity, idols and false prophets are swept away, and then the sword awakes against the LORD's own Shepherd: strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered. Jesus quoted this verse over His disciples on the night He was betrayed. The struck Shepherd and the opened fountain are two halves of one cross.
section.thesis: The fountain that cleanses sin is opened by the sword that strikes the Shepherd; the LORD wounds His own Companion so that a scattered, refined remnant may be washed, own His name, and be called His people.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the fountain opened for sin and uncleanness; the end of idols and false prophets, down to the prophet who denies his wounds; and the sword against the Shepherd, the sheep scattered, and a refined third brought through the fire to call on the LORD.

verses.text: “On that day a {{maqor|fountain}} will be opened to the house of David and the people of Jerusalem, to cleanse them from sin and {{niddah|impurity}}.

units.label: The end of idols and false prophets

verses.text: And on that day, declares the LORD of Hosts, I will erase the names of the idols from the land, and they will no longer be remembered. I will also remove the prophets and the spirit of impurity from the land.

And if anyone still prophesies, his father and mother who bore him will say to him, ‘You shall not remain alive, because you have spoken falsely in the name of the LORD.’ When he prophesies, his father and mother who bore him will pierce him through.
And on that day every prophet who prophesies will be ashamed of his vision, and he will not put on a hairy cloak in order to deceive.
He will say, ‘I am not a prophet; I work the land, for I was purchased as a servant in my youth.’
If someone asks him, ‘What are these wounds on your chest?’ he will answer, ‘These are the wounds I received in the house of my friends.’

units.label: The Shepherd struck, the sheep scattered
units.note: a third refined through the fire

verses.text: Awake, O sword, against My Shepherd, against the man who is My {{amit|Companion}}, declares the LORD of Hosts. Strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered, and I will turn My hand against the little ones.
And in all the land, declares the LORD, two-thirds will be cut off and perish, but a third will be left in it.

This third I will bring through the fire; I will {{tsaraph|refine}} them like silver and test them like gold. They will call on My name, and I will answer them. I will say, ‘They are My people,’ and they will say, ‘The LORD is our God.’”

maqor.gloss: A spring or fountain, the source from which water flows. Not a basin to be filled and emptied but a living, self-renewing source, opened for the house of David to wash away sin. The image answers the mourning of chapter 12: the very people who pierced the Lord are given a perpetual fountain of cleansing, opened, the New Testament shows, by His pierced side.

niddah.gloss: Impurity, defilement, the ritual uncleanness that barred a person from God's presence. Its use here says that sin is not merely guilt to be pardoned but filth to be washed; the fountain deals with both, cleansing from sin and from impurity, restoring the defiled to fellowship with a holy God.

amit.gloss: An associate, a near one, a fellow or companion who stands as an equal. Outside this verse the word appears almost entirely in Leviticus for one's neighbor and equal. For the LORD of Hosts to call the Shepherd the man who is My Companion is to set Him beside God as His peer, a staggering hint of the Shepherd's deity, fulfilled in the Son who is one with the Father.

tsaraph.gloss: To smelt, refine, or purify metal by fire, burning away the dross. The surviving third is not spared the fire but brought through it, refined like silver and tested like gold. Suffering here is not abandonment but the purifying hand of God, producing a people who call on His name and are answered as His own.

basic.context: The mourning of chapter 12 pours straight into cleansing. On that day God opens a fountain for the house of David to wash away sin and uncleanness. Then He purges the land of idols and false prophets, so thoroughly that a former prophet denies he ever was one and explains away the ritual gashes on his body. At the climax God calls a sword to awake against His own Shepherd, the man who is His Companion: strike the Shepherd, and the sheep scatter. Two-thirds perish, but a third is brought through the fire, refined, and restored as God's own people.
basic.hermeneutics: This is day of the LORD prophecy, tightly bound to chapter 12 and continued in chapter 14. The fountain and the struck Shepherd are read by the New Testament as fulfilled in Christ; Jesus Himself quotes verse 7 the night He is arrested. The main debate is the identity of the struck Shepherd, and whether verse 6 speaks of the false prophet's shame or, in an older reading, the wounds of Christ.
basic.originalLanguages: A maqor, a living fountain, is opened to cleanse from sin and from niddah, ritual impurity, so both guilt and defilement are washed away. The struck one is called the LORD's amit, His Companion or equal, a word used elsewhere almost only in Leviticus for a neighbor, hinting at the Shepherd's deity. And the surviving third is put through the fire and tsaraph, refined like silver, purified rather than destroyed.
basic.typology: The opened fountain foreshadows the cleansing flood from Christ's pierced side. The struck Shepherd whose sheep scatter is fulfilled in Gethsemane, quoted by Jesus over His fleeing disciples. The refined third that passes through fire and calls on God's name pictures the purified remnant, the church tested and owned as God's people.
basic.christ: Jesus applies verse 7 to Himself on the night of His betrayal: I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered, Matthew 26:31. The Shepherd called the LORD's Companion is the Son who is one with the Father, and the sword that awakes against Him is the just judgment God lays on Him in our place. The fountain of verse 1 is opened by that very stroke, so the struck Shepherd and the cleansing fountain are two sides of the one cross.
basic.god: God is holy: He purges idols, false prophets, and impurity, and He will not leave sin unaddressed. Yet He is astonishingly gracious: He opens a perpetual fountain for the guilty and refines a remnant through fire rather than destroying it. Most stunning of all, the sword falls by God's own command on His own Companion, so that the judgment sinners deserve lands on the Shepherd, and the scattered flock is gathered, cleansed, and owned as His people.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 26:31 quotes the struck Shepherd over the scattered disciples. John 19:34 shows blood and water from Jesus' pierced side, the fountain opened. 1 Peter 1:7 speaks of faith refined by fire like gold. Romans 9 to 11 traces the surviving, called remnant.
basic.oneStory: The mourning over the pierced One gives way to an opened fountain, and the fountain is opened by a sword that strikes God's own Shepherd. The flock scatters, but a refined remnant is brought through the fire to call on the LORD and be called His people. It all converges at Calvary, where the struck Shepherd bleeds the cleansing stream and gathers His scattered sheep.

context.literary:
Chapter 13 has no heading of its own because it is the second panel of the burden that began in 12:1. The words "on that day" in 13:1, 2 and 4 stitch it to what precedes, and the three movements are tightly ordered. Verse 1 is a single sentence of promise: a fountain opened. Verses 2 to 6 are about the clearing of the land, first of idols, then of prophets, then of the spirit of impurity that belongs with them. Verses 7 to 9 are a poem, set off by its own rhythm and by the heavy formula "declares the LORD of Hosts" (7), "declares the LORD" (8).

The middle section is a small drama in three scenes. The parents who would pierce their own son for false prophecy (3), the prophet who strips off the cloak and denies his calling (4 and 5), and the interrogation about the wounds on his chest (6). It moves from the family to the individual to a private conversation, and the answer in verse 6 is deliberately evasive. The poem that follows is by contrast direct and fierce, with commands in the second person to the sword and the shepherd, and numbers (two thirds, one third) that give it an almost legal finality.

There is a pattern of reversal in the chapter. The word "pierce" (daqar) turns up in 12:10 for the One whom the people pierced and in 13:3 for what loving parents will do to a false prophet. In the first, piercing is the offense for which grace is given; in the second, it is the zeal that cleanses the land. And the final promise, "They are My people," "The LORD is our God," completes the covenant formula that the whole book has been working toward.
context.historical:
The chapter assumes a world where false prophecy was still a live danger. The Persian-period community had seen prophets arise who spoke peace when God had not spoken, and Nehemiah 6:10-14 shows hired prophets trying to frighten the governor. The law had long ago set the penalty for a prophet who led people to other gods or spoke in God's name what He had not said (Deuteronomy 13:1-11 and 18:20). Parents who would carry out that penalty on their own child in verse 3 show a zeal for the LORD that overrides even the strongest natural tie, much as Deuteronomy 13:6-10 does when it requires a family member to refuse the enticer.

The hairy cloak of verse 4 was the garb of the prophet; Elijah wore such a garment (2 Kings 1:8) and John the Baptist later dressed in camel hair (Matthew 3:4). The point of the verse is that prophetic costume had become a means of deceit, and a time is coming when no one will want to wear it. The gashes on the chest in verse 6 recall self-wounding in pagan worship; the prophets of Baal cut themselves with swords and lances on Carmel (1 Kings 18:28), and the law forbade such cutting (Deuteronomy 14:1). A man pressed to explain such marks would be inclined to give an innocent account.

The numbers of verses 8 and 9 recall the thirds of Ezekiel 5:1-12, where a third of Jerusalem dies by plague, a third by the sword, and a third is scattered. Under Persian rule the community knew itself to be only a remnant of what Israel had been, and the promise that a refined third remains would have met their own experience of being a small, tested people.

The shepherd language reaches back into chapters 10 and 11, where Judah has bad shepherds and a good shepherd rejected for thirty pieces of silver (11:4-14), and a worthless shepherd who leaves the flock (11:15-17).
context.canonical:
The two great moves of the chapter, cleansing and a smitten shepherd, are taken up across the whole Bible. The fountain is the answer to the longing for purification that runs from the water of cleansing in Numbers 19 to Ezekiel 36:25, "I will also sprinkle clean water on you," and Psalm 51's cry to be washed. It leads to the living waters of 14:8 in the next chapter and to the river of life in Revelation 22.

The struck shepherd belongs to a line that begins with Moses and David as shepherds of the flock, passes through the bad shepherds of Ezekiel 34 and God's promise to shepherd the sheep Himself (Ezekiel 34:11-16, 23), and arrives at Jesus saying, "I am the good shepherd" (John 10:11). Isaiah 53:4-10 is the nearest parallel, the servant stricken and crushed by the will of the LORD for the sins of others. Zechariah 11:12-13, with its thirty pieces thrown into the house of the LORD, is the link between a rejected shepherd and the betrayal narrative in Matthew 26:14-16 and 27:3-10.

Jesus quotes verse 7 on the Mount of Olives, on the night of His arrest (Matthew 26:31, Mark 14:27, with the footnote noting the citation). He adds a promise that comes only in the Gospels: "after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee" (Matthew 26:32). Zechariah's scattering ends with a regathering that the Gospels show happening. The refining of the remnant is picked up in Malachi 3:2-3 and in 1 Peter 1:6-7, and the covenant formula that closes the chapter returns in Hosea 2:23, in Jeremiah 31:33, and in Revelation 21:3.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Zechariah wanted a community that had been wounded by false teaching to hear that God would deal with the sickness at its root and not simply tidy its symptoms. A lasting cleansing cannot be left to human reform; it has to be provided, and so a fountain is opened. The land must also be rid of voices that promise what God has not said, and the prophet describes that purge so severely that the former prophet is ashamed to admit his past, and his own family will not protect him.

The last three verses are given to people who may fear that such purity will leave no one standing. The answer is that God's way of refining is costly, that a great part will not survive, but that those who pass through the fire will be His and will know it. Zechariah means the hearers to face the cost without despair. The shepherd must be struck and the flock must be scattered before the covenant is renewed, and the hearers are to see that God Himself commands the blow, not as an accident of history but as the way the cleansing fountain is opened.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is prediction, not instruction. The parents who pierce a prophet are described as part of what the day will look like and are not given as a model for how families should treat those who err. The Old Testament law had a penalty for false prophecy, but the New Testament does not carry it over into the church, and no reader should take verse 3 as permission to harm anyone. Jesus warns of false prophets (Matthew 7:15) and tells His disciples to recognize them by their fruit, not by violence.

What does carry over is the seriousness. Truth about God matters enough that those closest to a teacher are expected to refuse him when he lies in God's name. The chapter also supports an ordinary pastoral habit: sin is to be named and brought to the fountain, and those who have been burned in the fire are not to be treated as spent. The refining of the third is a promise for those who are suffering now.

debates.question: Who is the Shepherd struck in verse 7?

views.label: The Messiah, Christ Himself
views.case: Jesus quotes the verse of His own arrest (Matthew 26:31), and the title My Companion sets the Shepherd beside God as an equal. The sword is summoned by the LORD, the substitution at the heart of the cross, and the chapter's fountain is opened by the stroke.

views.label: A faithless or rejected shepherd under judgment
views.case: Because chapter 11 has both a good shepherd and a worthless one, some argue that the struck shepherd is a leader God removes in judgment so that the flock is tested. The fact that the scattering falls on the sheep fits a bad shepherd as easily as a good one.

views.label: A representative shepherd who stands for the leaders of the people
views.case: A few read the figure as the royal or priestly leadership as a class, struck down so that the people can be purified. Even those who hold this view usually grant that the New Testament applies the verse to Christ.

debates.bearing: Matthew and Mark put the verse on Jesus' own lips as the explanation of what is happening that night. The Hebrew has an imperative to the sword, while Matthew gives the first person, I will strike, which makes explicit that God is the one acting.

debates.question: What are the wounds in verse 6?

views.label: The self-inflicted marks of a false prophet
views.case: In context the man is trying to hide his former calling, and the marks on his chest fit the ritual gashes of pagan prophecy (1 Kings 18:28). He lies about the cause, saying he was hurt in a friend's house.

views.label: A reference to the wounds of Christ
views.case: Some Christian readers have taken the verse as a prophecy of the cross, since the Hebrew says literally wounds between your hands and the word for friends is built on the verb to love, so the wounding comes from those who loved Him.

views.label: Wounds of discipline from friends or family
views.case: Others take the wounds as marks of the parental discipline of verse 3, a beating by family which he turns to cover his shame.

debates.bearing: The immediate context favors the false prophet, and the connection to Christ is a later reading and not an apostolic one. The New Testament nowhere quotes verse 6, but it does quote verse 7, which is the surer ground.

study.originalLanguages:
Maqor, "fountain" (13:1). The word means a spring that flows from the ground, and it is the word Jeremiah 2:13 uses for the fountain of living waters that the people forsook. What they abandoned, God opens again. In Psalm 36:9 the psalmist says that with God is the fountain of life. The verb "opened" (patach) suggests a source that has been shut, and the form in Zechariah is passive: someone else does the opening. The fountain is not dug by those it cleanses.

Chattat and niddah, "sin" and "impurity" (13:1). The first is the common word for sin and for a sin offering; the second belongs to the vocabulary of ritual separation, used of the impurity of a menstruating woman (Leviticus 12:2) and of the water for impurity made with the ashes of a red heifer (Numbers 19:9). Together the two words cover moral guilt and the uncleanness that keeps a person from the presence of God. Zechariah promises that one fountain will deal with both.

Ruach hatumah, "the spirit of impurity" (13:2). The footnote reads "the unclean spirit." It is paired with the idols and the false prophets, which suggests that the three belong together as a power behind false worship. It is the phrase the Gospels use again and again for demons, whom Jesus casts out.

Geber amiti, "the man who is My Companion" (13:7). Geber is a strong man, a person of stature. Amit is a rare word. Outside this verse it belongs to the language of Leviticus, where it speaks of a fellow member of the community, a near neighbor (Leviticus 18:20, 19:15, 25:14). The word implies closeness, a person of one's own kind. Here God says it of the one who is to be struck, which is why the verse has so often been read as a hint of the Shepherd's nearness to God.

Tsaraph and bachan, "refine" and "test" (13:9). Tsaraph is the word for smelting silver and for the refiner's work, while bachan is to assay or test the metal. They are used together in Psalm 66:10 ("You refined us like silver") and in Malachi 3:2-3, where the Lord sits as a refiner. The process is not destruction; the point of fire is to separate what is true from the dross.

The closing exchange of verse 9 is a covenant formula, "They are My people... The LORD is our God," the same pairing that appears in Exodus 6:7 and Hosea 2:23.

typology.fulfillment: The fountain for sin and impurity looks ahead to the blood and water from Christ's side, John 19:34, and to the cleansing blood of 1 John 1:7 and Hebrews 9:13-14, which does what the ashes of the heifer could only picture. The escalation is from ritual water that cleansed the outside to a cleansing of the conscience. Titus 3:5 speaks of the washing of new birth. The type falls short in that the water of Numbers 19 had to be applied again and again, while Hebrews 10:10-14 says the one offering of Christ has made perfect forever those who are being sanctified.

typology.type: The Shepherd struck and the sheep scattered
typology.fulfillment: On the night of His arrest Jesus took verse 7 as His own, Matthew 26:31 and Mark 14:27, and the disciples fled (Mark 14:50, John 16:32). He is the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11, and the great shepherd brought back from the dead through the blood of the eternal covenant, Hebrews 13:20. The escalation is from the loss of a leader to a leader's willing death. The type falls short because Zechariah's scattering is a catastrophe, and in the gospel the scattering is followed by the regathering Jesus promised in Matthew 26:32.

A remnant brought through fire and called God's own is a picture of the church tested by trial, 1 Peter 1:6-7 and 4:12, and of the remnant that Paul says is saved by grace, Romans 11:5. The words of 13:9, They are My people, reappear in 1 Peter 2:10 of a people who were once not a people. The escalation is that the covenant formula is spoken to Jew and Gentile together in Christ. The type is incomplete in its arithmetic: Zechariah gives a third, and in the gospel there is no number that excludes anyone who calls on His name.

typology.type: The prophet who denies his calling
typology.fulfillment: The false prophet who disowns his past in shame is a negative image of Peter in the courtyard, who denied his Lord three times (Luke 22:54-62), and was restored beside a fire of coals (John 21:15-17). The contrast lies in what is denied. The false prophet denies a lie, and Peter denied the truth. The type falls short because Zechariah's man hides his shame, whereas Peter was brought to say, 'You know I love You', and was commissioned again.

study.christ:
Few verses in the Old Testament are quoted by Jesus with so little change. On the way to Gethsemane He says, "This very night you will all fall away on account of Me," and cites Zechariah to explain why: "I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered" (Matthew 26:31). The Hebrew of verse 7 is a command to the sword, "Awake," and Jesus puts God's own hand behind it, I will strike. That shift is the key. He does not describe the coming hours as a tragedy that overtakes Him, but as an act of God, foretold, and aimed at Him.

The title "My Companion," amit, adds weight. A God who calls a man His near equal is saying something that no prophet's biography could carry. When Jesus takes this verse to Himself, He takes the title too, which is consistent with His claims in John 10:30 and 14:9. The Shepherd struck is the Shepherd who is close to God, and the sword that wakes against Him is the judgment God has laid on the One standing in the sinners' place, as Isaiah 53:6 and 10 say.

The fountain of verse 1 is not separate from the stroke of verse 7. In the order of the chapter the cleansing comes first, but in the order of events it comes because of the stroke. John sees blood and water come from the side of the Shepherd when He is pierced (19:34), and the First Letter of John draws the conclusion that the blood of Jesus purifies us from all sin (1 John 1:7). The word for purifying there carries both of Zechariah's categories, guilt and defilement.

The scattering is not the end. In the same breath in which Jesus quotes the verse He promises, "after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee" (Matthew 26:32). The pattern of Zechariah 13 is struck, scattered, refined, called, owned, and in the Gospels the whole pattern is lived out within a few days. The one who is struck is also the one who gathers.

A caution should be kept. The verse is about a struck shepherd, and the New Testament quotes it that way. It does not follow that every detail of the chapter is a hidden portrait of Jesus. The wounds of verse 6, for instance, are better understood in their own setting, and the connection to the cross there is not one the apostles draw. The fountain and the shepherd are on firmer ground, because Jesus Himself and John point to them.
study.god:
The chapter shows God as holy in a way that is impossible to ignore. He erases the names of idols so completely that they will no longer be remembered (13:2), a more thorough work than smashing them. He removes the prophets who speak in His name falsely and the spirit of impurity that sits behind them. He will not leave a lie standing in His own name, and the zeal He asks of parents in verse 3 is only a small echo of His own.

Yet the same chapter opens with the plainest mercy. A fountain is opened, and it is opened for the house of David and the people of Jerusalem, the very people who have just been mourning the One they pierced. God does not delay cleansing until the guilty can earn it. He opens the source first. There is a tension here that Scripture does not hide: the God who purges the land is the God who pours out grace, and the second makes the first bearable.

The central verse presses the tension to its limit. God calls the sword to wake against His own Shepherd, the man who is His Companion. This is not a God who stands apart from the cost of sin and sends someone else to pay it. The One struck is near to Him, and the blow is His decision. Isaiah 53:10 says it was the LORD's will to crush Him. No account of the doctrine of God can leave this out: His justice is real, His love is real, and in the stroke they meet. Christian teaching holds that the Son goes to the cross willingly (John 10:17-18), so that the Father's command and the Son's gift are one act.

The last verses reveal how God handles His people when He disciplines them. Two thirds are cut off, a third is brought through fire. The refiner does not walk away from the crucible; He watches, because He is after silver and gold. And what He is after is not only moral improvement but a relationship, a people who call on His name and receive an answer, and who say what He says of them: "They are My people." "The LORD is our God." The God of this chapter is jealous for His name and also jealous for His people.

For worship this brings reverence and confidence together. Believers can be sober about the seriousness of sin because the chapter will not let them be casual, and they can be joyful because the fountain stays open. It also changes how suffering is read: a believer's fire is the refiner's work, not abandonment.

crossReferences.note: Jesus quotes verse 7 on the way to Gethsemane and attaches a promise: after He is raised He will go ahead of the scattered disciples into Galilee. Zechariah's scattering ends in a regathering, and Jesus names the place.

Mark gives the same quotation and the same promise, and the disciples' flight in 14:50 shows the scattering taking place within hours. The verse is not an abstract oracle for Jesus; He applies it to the people sitting with Him.

The soldier pierces Jesus' side and blood and water flow out. Read with Zechariah 13:1, the two together present the cross as the place where the fountain for sin and impurity is opened, and the blood and water as the two aspects, atonement and cleansing, that Zechariah joined.

It was the LORD's will to crush the Servant and make His soul a guilt offering. The same note sounds in Zechariah 13:7, where it is God who rouses the sword. Both passages insist that the wounding of God's chosen one is God's own purpose and not an accident.

The water of impurity made with the ashes of the red heifer is the Old Testament's provision for the very uncleanness (niddah) Zechariah names. The fountain promised here does permanently what that water had to do again and again.

The law demanded that even a close relative be refused, and not shielded, when he tried to draw a person away from the LORD. Zechariah 13:3 shows the same loyalty at its fullest, when parents themselves act against a false prophet. It explains why the zeal described is seen as faithfulness and not cruelty.

The shepherd's wages of thirty pieces of silver, thrown to the potter in the house of the LORD, are the other side of this chapter's struck Shepherd. The rejected shepherd of chapter 11 and the struck shepherd of chapter 13 are drawn by Matthew into the betrayal and passion of Jesus.

The Lord who comes to His temple is like a refiner's fire and sits as a refiner and purifier of silver. It is the same imagery as Zechariah 13:9, and it shows that God's fire is meant to purify the sons of Levi and the people, not to destroy them.

Peter says that trials prove the genuineness of faith, more precious than gold that perishes though refined by fire. It carries Zechariah's test of the third into the life of the church: suffering is the means by which God makes believers fit to call on Him.

God says to those who were not His people, You are My people, and they answer, You are my God. The exchange matches the end of Zechariah 13:9 almost exactly, and Paul and Peter take it up for the church (Romans 9:25-26, 1 Peter 2:10).

study.oneStory:
The question this chapter answers goes back to the beginning. Genesis 3 ends with a man and woman sent out of the garden and a sword guarding the way to the tree of life (3:24). Ever since, the problem of the Bible has been how sinners can come back to the presence of God. The sacrificial law gave a partial answer, with its washings, its sin offerings, and its water of impurity. The prophets said the answer had to go deeper, and Ezekiel 36:25-27 promised clean water and a new spirit. Zechariah sharpens the promise into a place: a fountain, opened.

What Zechariah adds is the cost, and it is a surprise. The cleansing comes through a shepherd struck by the sword of the LORD. The story of Israel has been the story of shepherds who failed, the kings and priests who led the flock astray, and of the God who said He would shepherd the sheep Himself (Ezekiel 34:15). Zechariah shows how: the true Shepherd takes the blow that the flock deserved. The line then runs through Isaiah 53 to Gethsemane and to Golgotha, where a soldier's spear opens a side and blood and water flow.

Between the promise and its fulfillment lies the long refining of the people of God. Exile, return, the silent centuries, the persecution of the first Christians, the trials of every generation of the church: Zechariah says that these are the fire, and that God's goal is a people who call on His name and hear Him answer. Revelation 21:3 gives that goal its last form: the dwelling of God is with men, they are His people, and God Himself is with them.

So the chapter sits at the center of the story's turn from judgment to renewal. The land is cleansed of idols, which Genesis 3 began and the prophets longed to see ended, and the covenant formula that was spoken at Sinai is spoken again, this time as a promise answered. The creation story ends with a tree of life guarded by a sword. The new creation story begins with a Shepherd under the sword and a fountain opened.

sermon.title: There Shall Be a Fountain Opened
sermon.why: Piper preaches Zechariah 13:1 as the most important promise in the book, arguing that the old sacrifices could not take away sin and that the fountain still to be opened was the pierced side of the Son of God, into which he draws the mourning over the pierced One of 12:10; a careful, Christ-centered exposition of this passage.

quiz.q: What is opened on that day, and for what purpose?

options.text: A fountain, to cleanse the house of David from sin and impurity.
options.note: Verse 1: a fountain opened to wash away sin and uncleanness.

options.text: A treasury, to make the people wealthy.
options.note: The fountain is for cleansing from sin, not for riches.

options.text: A gate, to let the nations invade.
options.note: The image is a cleansing fountain, not an open gate.

options.text: Nothing of lasting significance.
options.note: The fountain is the foundation of every other promise in the book.

quiz.q: Who is the Shepherd struck by the sword in verse 7?

options.text: The LORD's own Companion, applied by Jesus to Himself at His arrest.
options.note: Jesus quotes this verse in Matthew 26:31 of His own striking.

options.text: A foreign general defeated in battle.
options.note: The struck one is the LORD's Companion, fulfilled in Christ.

options.text: One of the false prophets of verse 2.
options.note: The Shepherd is God's equal, not a false prophet.

options.text: No one; it is only poetic imagery.
options.note: Jesus treats it as a real prophecy fulfilled in Him.

quiz.q: What does the title My Companion reveal about the Shepherd?

options.text: He stands beside God as His equal, a hint of the Shepherd's deity.
options.note: Amit denotes a near equal, setting the Shepherd at God's own side.

options.text: He is merely a hired hand with no special standing.
options.note: The word marks Him as God's equal, not a hireling.

options.text: He is an enemy of God.
options.note: He is God's Companion, struck by God's own command for the sheep.

options.text: The title means nothing in particular.
options.note: It is a striking claim to the Shepherd's equality with God.

quiz.q: What happens to the surviving third of the people?

options.text: They are brought through the fire, refined, and owned as God's people.
options.note: Verse 9: refined like silver, calling on God, called His own.

options.text: They are spared all hardship and left untested.
options.note: They are refined through fire, not spared it.

options.text: They are cut off along with the rest.
options.note: The third is preserved and purified, not cut off.

options.text: They are abandoned by God forever.
options.note: God calls them His people and answers when they call.

quiz.q: How are the fountain and the struck Shepherd related?

options.text: The fountain of cleansing is opened by the sword that strikes the Shepherd, both fulfilled at the cross.
options.note: The struck Shepherd's pierced side pours out the cleansing stream.

options.text: They are unrelated events far apart in time.
options.note: The chapter binds them as two sides of one saving act.

options.text: The fountain washes away the need for any Shepherd.
options.note: The fountain flows precisely because the Shepherd is struck.

options.text: The Shepherd blocks the fountain from the people.
options.note: The Shepherd's striking is what opens the fountain.

questions: A fountain was opened for sin and impurity. Are you still trying to wash yourself, or have you come to the fountain God has opened in Christ?
God purged idols and false prophets from the land. What false voices or hidden idols is God calling you to let Him remove?
The sword fell on the Shepherd in your place. How does it change your view of the cross to see that God struck His own Companion for you?
The remnant was refined, not spared, by fire. Where is God using trial to purify rather than to punish you, and can you trust His hand in it?
The struck Shepherd gathers scattered sheep. Where have you scattered from Him, and how does His promise to gather you draw you back?

translationNotes.note: Fountain renders maqor, a living spring or source, not a mere pool; it is opened, an ongoing, sufficient supply of cleansing rather than a one-time washing.

Wounds on your chest translates a phrase meaning literally between your hands; in context it describes the exposed false prophet, though its wording has long been applied devotionally to the wounds of Christ.
My Companion renders amit, a word used almost only in Leviticus for a near equal or neighbor; here it marks the Shepherd as God's peer, and Jesus applies the verse to Himself in Matthew 26:31.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Zechariah 13:1-9. All 9 verses reproduced in order. footnote markers omitted from the running text.
